text: El Anatsui, born on 4 February 1944 in Anyako, in the Volta Region of Ghana, is a Ghanaian sculptor who has spent much of his career in Nigeria. He gained international recognition for his "bottle-top installations," which consist of thousands of aluminum pieces collected from alcohol recycling stations and sewn together with copper wire to form metallic, cloth-like wall sculptures. Though the materials appear stiff and sturdy, they are actually flexible, which aids in installation. Anatsui was included in the 2023 Time 100 list of the world's most influential people, with art historian Okeke-Agulu noting that his work transforms ordinary materials like printer’s plates or liquor-bottle caps into magnificent, globally displayed compositions. The youngest of his father’s 32 children, Anatsui lost his mother and was raised by his uncle; his first artistic experience was drawing letters on a chalkboard, which his school headmaster encouraged, and he viewed the forms as images rather than letters. He earned a B.A. in 1968 and a postgraduate diploma in Art Education in 1969, both from the College of Art and Built Environment (KNUST) in Kumasi. Influenced by artists like Oku Ampofo, Vincent Akwete Kofi, and Kofi Antubam, who rejected foreign influences in favor of indigenous art, Anatsui taught at Winneba Specialist Training College (now University of Education) after graduating and later moved to the University of Nigeria, Nsukka in 1975, becoming a senior lecturer in 1982, head of the Fine and Applied Arts department and full professor of sculpture in 1996, a role he held until 2011. He is affiliated with the Nsukka group and has built a global reputation while living and working in Nsukka. Anatsui noted that his education emphasized Western art, lacking focus on African culture, prompting him to visit the National Cultural Centre in Kumasi, where he encountered Adinkra, a system of signs and symbols, which introduced him to abstract art. In the 1970s, he worked in wood, carving trays and creating wall panels with Adinkra symbols and designs using hot rods, chain saws, gouges, flame, or paint. In the late 1970s, he began working in clay, exploring themes of fragility and transformation, particularly in broken pots that he saw as acquiring spiritual uses for ancestors and deities. He later explored food-related materials such as mortars and bottle tops. Much of his work uses found materials, emphasizing their history of use and the human hand’s imprint; he believes used objects carry energy from those who touched them, grounding his art in culture and environment. Bottle caps are especially favored because they resemble cloth, allowing both sculptural and painterly interpretations, and they reflect political and sociological contexts through brand names and colors. He sees the transformation of these materials—removed from their functional roles—as a way to generate reflection, thought, or wonder. Themes in his work include the destruction and reconstitution of materials as a metaphor for Africa’s colonial and post-colonial history, traditional West African textile motifs, and resistance to Western misinterpretations of African history. The concept of Sankofa ("go back and retrieve") is central to his practice, representing a return to African cultural roots as a path to self-discovery. His career began in Nsukka and expanded to Enugu, Lagos, and internationally. In 1990, he had his first major group show at the Studio Museum in Harlem and was featured in the exhibition "Contemporary African Artists: Changing Traditions," which ran for five years. He has exhibited globally, including at the Brooklyn Museum (2013), Clark Art Institute (2011), Rice University Art Gallery (2010), Metropolitan Museum of Art (2008–09), National Museum of African Art (Smithsonian, 2008), Fowler Museum (UCLA, 2007), Venice Biennale (1990 and 2007), Hayward Gallery (2005), Liverpool Biennial (2002), and the Arab Museum of Modern Art (2019) and Kunstmuseum Bern (2020). In 1995, he held his first solo exhibition outside Africa in London, where he demonstrated African art in non-traditional, conceptually rich ways. In 2005, he appeared in the permanent collection at the de Young Museum in San Francisco and had his first display of metal sheets at Skoto Gallery in New York, which popularized his bottle-cap works. In 2006 and 2007, he was invited to the Venice Biennale, where he created two hanging metal tapestries displayed at Palazzo Fortuny, including Dusasa, which featured golds, reds, and blacks and created a gentle, unique aesthetic. Art curator Robert Storr described the series as exalting and distinct from postwar European art. Anatsui began referring to his metal works as "hangings" rather than "cloths" during this period. A 2010 retrospective, "When I Last Wrote to You About Africa," opened at the Royal Ontario Museum and toured the U.S. for three years. A major exhibition, "Gravity & Grace: Monumental Works by El Anatsui," premiered at the Brooklyn Museum in 2013 and traveled to the Des Moines Art Center (2013–14) and the Bass Museum of Art (2014). A career-spanning survey, "Triumphant Scale," organized by Okwui Enwezor and Chika Okeke-Agulu, opened in March 2019 at Haus der Kunst in Munich and traveled to the Arab Museum of Modern Art (Doha) and Kunstmuseum Bern (2020). In 2023, Anatsui was selected for the Hyundai Commission at Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall, where his work "Behind the Red Moon," made from thousands of metal bottle tops and fragments, addresses the transatlantic slave trade and will be on view through April 14, 2024. He was elected to the International Society for Education through Art (InSEA) world council in 1992, a founding member and fellow of the Forum for African Arts in 2000, and a member of the International Selection Committee for the Dakar Biennale in 2000. He was a fellow at the Civitella Ranieri Foundation in 2001. Anatsui won an honorable mention at the First Ghana National Art Competition in 1968 and was named Best Student of the Year at KNUST in 1969. In 1983, he received a commission for two large terrazzo-surfaced cement sculptures on the Nsukka campus. In 1984, he was invited to the Zweites Symposium Nordesekkuste residency in Cuxhaven, West Germany. In 1990, he received an honorable mention at the 44th Venice Biennale and was included in the documentary Nigerian Art-Kindred Spirits. In 2015, he was awarded the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at the Venice Biennale, and in 2017, he received the Praemium Imperiale, becoming the first Ghanaian to win this international art prize.
